candidates.buyer: Pawnshops and casas de prestamo/empeno (small, often family-run) in La Paz, El Alto, Cochabamba and other cities

candidates.unchecked: Whether the AEMP has a current register, pledge-book or reporting duties after 2018. Whether any 2025-26 rule exists. Size of the current universe. No local-language competitor search done (budget used).

candidates.unchecked: Any periodic reporting to ASFI or UIF. The buyer group is tiny and the duty is a board and a spread, so little software need.

coverage.category: 1. Household employers: domestic workers, live-in carers, nannies
coverage.found: No Bolivian rule found requiring household employers to register workers on a platform. Only an undated eju.tv note on a Mintrabajo resolution under ILO C189 (written contract, wage booklet/libreta). The 2026 salary-minimum payroll complement (Bs 3,300, deadline 15 Apr 2026, via OVT) targets firms. Nothing new beyond K03.

coverage.category: 2. Scrap-metal dealers
coverage.found: No Bolivian scrap-dealer register or traceability rule found. Only gold-scrap export control by Senarecom (see gold candidate).

coverage.category: 3. Second-hand dealers and pawnbrokers
coverage.found: Pawnshops and loan houses: ASFI census in 2018 (about 350 registered), then ASFI said they fall under the AEMP; licence and matricula there. No 2025-26 rule found. Used-phone dealers: IMEI registry (DS 0353/2009) binds users and operators, with no dealer-level duty found. See the pawnshop candidate.

coverage.category: 4. Gold and jewellery buyers
coverage.found: BCB approved a new internal gold-purchase regulation (4 Dec 2025, reported as Res. 091/2026); Law 1503/2023 makes selling to the BCB mandatory. DS 29165 requires NIM, the Formulario Unico de Exportacion and reporting to Senarecom. Gold smuggling cases are making news. Jewellery shops not searched.

coverage.category: 5. Used car parts and vehicle dismantlers
coverage.found: No Bolivian dismantler or parts-traceability rule found (the only autoparts hit was Argentine).

coverage.category: 6. Livestock traders, markets and animal transport
coverage.found: The SENASAG Guia de Movimiento Animal (GMA) is mandatory and free, issued through the state system Gran Paititi (DS 29251/2007, Igarape report Feb 2026). Brands and signs are kept by ranchers' associations (DS 28303). No fair/market licensing rule found. A free state system exists.

coverage.category: 7. Small abattoirs and butchers
coverage.found: SENASAG regulation on sanitary registration of mataderos and construction authorisation exists (FAOLEX), with older deadline extensions; mobile slaughter units revised under DS 3639. No butcher-level rule found.

coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: Only found that the GMA covers moving bees. No dedicated beekeeper register or levy found; thin screen (no dedicated search).

coverage.category: 9. Veterinary practices and veterinary medicine sellers
coverage.found: SENASAG regulation on veterinary companies (makers, importers, distributors, sellers of vet products). Nothing new beyond K04.

coverage.category: 10. Well drillers and water abstraction
coverage.found: Water-use authorisation is granted jointly with the service licence by AAPS (and SENARI for irrigation). NB 173001 (well construction) and SIASBO (groundwater information system) exist. No driller register or permit procedure confirmed.

coverage.category: 11. Septic, sanitation and waste haulers
coverage.found: Ley 755 (2015) is the framework. PAHO is supporting an update of the health-facility waste regulation (Jul 2025). Haulers' licence and reporting duties not confirmed.

coverage.category: 12. Lift, boiler and pressure-equipment owners and inspectors
coverage.found: No Bolivian lift or boiler inspection regime found (results were Spanish and Argentine). Only a TUV Bolivia lift-inspection service page appeared. Treat as probably no mandatory regime, unverified.

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: AAPS licences and registers EPSAs, including community committees. RAR 515/2017 guide has forms for under 10,000 and under 2,000 inhabitants. AAPS targeted 25 EPSAs to regularise in 2025 (54 done in 2024 per its report). Five-year plans (PDQ) and transitional plans (PTDS) are required. See the candidate.

coverage.category: 14. Pesticide and fertiliser dealers and applicators
coverage.found: SENASAG RA 7/2017 (regulation for pesticide registration and control, CAN Decision 804) requires registration of firms that sell, package, distribute and apply pesticides; RA 40/2018 requires sellers and distributors to register. Several 2024 RAs (227, 250, 275) were seen but not opened. Applicator-level duties not confirmed.

coverage.category: 15. Labour contractors and recruitment agencies
coverage.found: Private employment agencies must register with Mintrabajo (RM 1321/18 and 108/19; Law 263 art. 25; DS 1486 art. 18). No 2025-26 outsourcing decree found.

coverage.category: 16. Cemeteries, burial societies and funeral services
coverage.found: The search returned only foreign results. No Bolivian cemetery or funeral rule found; municipal ordinances under Ley 482 are likely but unchecked. Screened as unverified.

coverage.category: 17. Community and religious bodies: associations, charities, halal and kosher supervision
coverage.found: Legal personality for entities active in more than one department is granted by the Ministerio de la Presidencia / Viceministerio de Autonomias (Law 351 as amended by Law 915; RM 195/2025). One department: the gobernacion. Pre-Law-351 entities must adapt statutes (DS 3746, RM 51/19). No annual-report duty found. Halal/kosher not applicable.

coverage.category: 18. Transport operators: minibus, taxi, moto-taxi, small trucking and bus fleets
coverage.found: The police ITV and SOAT are annual for all vehicles. The 2025 deadline was 31 Dec 2025 after an extension; Bs 100 fine; police checks from 1 Jan 2026; more than 150 inspection points. No operator-specific ATT licence renewal found. Vehicle-by-vehicle compliance calendar is the only angle.

coverage.category: 19. Market traders, street vendors, money changers
coverage.found: ASFI runs a 2026 control plan on casas de cambio: price boards must be visible, buy-sell spread at most Bs 0.10 against the BCB official rate, unlicensed shops closed; 183 licensed in Jul 2024. Fintech/crypto firms had a 30 Apr 2026 deadline to file a letter of intent. Market traders and street vendors not searched.

coverage.category: 20. Small licensed premises with inspections: tattoo studios, driving schools, childminders and nurseries, small food producers, hunting outfitters
coverage.found: Nurseries: SEDEGES 2009 accreditation regulation; national guidelines for opening, accreditation and closure drafted in 2023-2025, not confirmed as approved. Driving schools: SEGELIC issues licences, and no school-authorisation regime found. Front-of-pack labelling: Law 775 has never been regulated, and Senate bill 042/2022-23 is pending. Tattoo studios and hunting outfitters: not searched.

coverage.category: 21. Fuel stations and fuel or LPG distributors
coverage.found: Sales reporting is K08 (state B-SISA). New 2026 regime: DS 5644 (June 2026) allows private diesel/gasoline imports; stations must keep YPFB and imported product segregated, importers must register volumes and per-lot analyses in ANH systems (Art. 14), buyers over 120 L need DGSC registration/authorization (Art. 15-16). Decree takes effect only when an ANH resolution is published; implementing ministerial resolution not found. DS 5534/5517 (Jan 2026) cover GLP pricing and diesel sales by ID only. No GLP-bottler reporting rule found.

coverage.category: 22. Grain, coffee, cocoa and other commodity traders, millers and warehouses
coverage.found: SENASAG RA 057/2019 requires registration of collection, processing and packing centres for plant-product exports. Nothing newer found for grain warehouses. EUDR is K07. Weak, unverified.

coverage.category: 23. Co-operatives, credit unions and savings groups
coverage.found: ASFI lists savings and credit co-operatives dropped from the adequacy process (data to 31 Oct 2025); no new reporting rule found. Mining co-operatives have an annual 31 January filing to AFCOOP (Ley 1140 Art. 3), see candidate.

coverage.category: 24. Private clinics, labs and other health providers that bill insurers or state schemes
coverage.found: No 2026 rule found on CNS billing agreements or private-clinic reporting. Only the general SNIS epidemiological notification (forms 302a/302b) and DS 4205 (2020). Nothing actionable.

coverage.category: 25. Pharmacies, medicine importers, and users of controlled chemicals or precursors
coverage.found: Ministry of Health controlled-substances manual (AGEMED T-N-22) covers pharmacies, clinics and distributors. AGEMED online platform reported down since 2 June 2026 (Cifabol), blocking registrations and customs clearance, which hits importers. DGSC chemicals is K01. Pharmacy narcotics ledger not verified.

coverage.category: 26. Security, cleaning and manpower agencies, and the firms that hire their workers
coverage.found: Private security is regulated by Denacev (Police); no 2026 rule found. Payroll duties (OVT supplementary minimum-wage payroll, deadline 15 April 2026, DGTHSO-014/26) fall under K03. Nothing new.

coverage.category: 27. Construction, mining and quarry contractors and suppliers: site registers, accreditation, local-content reports
coverage.found: Mining co-operatives with mining rights must file annual report or financial statements plus a notarised member list by 31 January, with fines, a trading ban and suspension for non-filing (Ley 845; Ley 1140 moved filing to AFCOOP). A 2018 AJAM account showed 408 of 581 co-operatives filed nothing. Mining patent debt is being collected through the courts (first coercive-collection ruling against a gold co-operative). No construction site register found.

coverage.category: 28. Notaries, land agents, real estate brokers and other professionals with periodic or anti-money-laundering reports
coverage.found: UIF made notaries reporting subjects (Res. 084/2018); a later report limits it to cash over US$300,000. Nothing found for 2025-26 or for real-estate agents or exchange houses. Low volume, weak.

coverage.category: 29. Hotels, guest houses and short-term rentals: guest registers, tourism levies
coverage.found: DS 4574 (2021) Art. 35: lodgings must send foreign guests' data to Migración via web at registration (24 hours if there is no stable internet); agencies must send it immediately (Art. 34). SIN requires the SIAT Hoteles module (RND 102000000030). No fine stated in the decree. No third-party PMS integration found.

result.competitor: I found no private compliance software. The core filing (Art. 14 lot registration) is made directly in the ANH's own systems. Under DS 5218, quality specifications are already submitted digitally with an electronic signature, and authorisation takes at most 5 working days through YPFB no-objection, then DGSC, then ANH resolution. B-SISA (the K08 killer) covers sales reporting. For a solo-founder tool, the state system does most of the job. Customs brokers and law firms (for example Ferrere, PixiLegal) handle the paperwork.
result.duty: DS 5644 (29 Jun 2026) is Bolivian law. Art. 10 lets stations and puestos de venta sell YPFB fuel alongside privately imported fuel, but only if they keep infrastructure, volume, storage and price separate as an ANH resolution will set out. Art. 12 bans reselling or mixing YPFB product. Art. 14 makes authorised importers register volumes and the full quality analysis for each lot in ANH systems before the fuel enters the country. Art. 17-18 set fines of UFV 2,000 (minor), 5,000 (serious) and 10,000 (very serious), and allow the operating licence or import authorisation to be revoked. Importers selling under 5,000 L must become a service station under DS 24721. The Disposición Final Primera says the decree takes effect only once the ANH Administrative Resolution is published. That should have come within about 25 working days via a Ministerial Resolution, but I could not find it published. The only 2026 ANH resolution I found was RAN-ANH-DJ-UGJN 0031/2026 of 24 Jul, on preventive intervention, and only through an opinion column. So it is unconfirmed whether the decree is in force. The duty applies per import lot, so frequency depends on how often a firm imports. DS 5701 was not found.
result.market: The market is very small. In Jan-Oct 2025 the ANH authorised 98 private importers: 72 for own consumption and 26 for resale (eju.tv, 12 Oct 2025). In 2024 there were 18. I found no 2026 count, and I found no figure for how many stations sell imported fuel. Bolivia has a few thousand service stations in total, but most sell only YPFB product. The DS 5644 regime is new and its uptake is unknown.
result.reason: The duty is real in the text of DS 5644, but it starts only when an ANH resolution is published, and I found no trace of that resolution. So I cannot confirm the duty is in force. The core filing is lot registration in ANH's own systems, and quality documents already go in digitally with an electronic signature, so software adds little. The buyer pool is tiny: 98 authorised importers in 2025, 26 of them for resale, with no 2026 count. The station segregation rules depend on an ANH resolution I could not find. Buyers could pay, but the market is too small and too uncertain, and the rules keep changing under the emergency decrees. Revisit if the ANH publishes detailed segregation and reporting rules for stations.

result.competitor: Searches for a software product, a state online portal (AFCOOP/AJAM) or a co-operative accounting system in Bolivia found none. The real substitute is the co-op's own accountant plus a notary. AJAM publishes a paper form (FormularioCF-01-01).
result.duty: Ley 1140 (21 Dec 2018) Art. 3: mining co-operatives holding mining rights must file with AFCOOP by 31 January of the following year. The filing is the annual report or financial statements, plus an updated member list certified by a notary. Non-filing brings fines under Ley 356 and its regulating decree; no amounts were found. Ley 1140 repealed Ley 845 Arts. 2-6, so the claim's "Ley 845 Art. 4" no longer applies. DS 2889 (2016) and the AJAM control regulation also set a 31 January filing, to AJAM, with trading bans and suspension. Whether these still apply, and whether AFCOOP or AJAM receives the filing, is unverified because Ley 1140 repeals "disposiciones contrarias" (anything that contradicts it). The obligation is annual. I found no news on enforcement after 2018.
result.market: Estimates of how many mining co-operatives exist conflict. eju.tv (Sept 2025) says 3,383 are formally registered. A Ministry of Mining figure reported by eju.tv gives 2,388 co-ops with 135,436 members. CONCOBOL says 1,666. None of these is an official AJAM/AFCOOP register count for 2025.
result.reason: The duty is real. Ley 1140 Art. 3 (in force, 2018) requires mining co-operatives to file by 31 January each year with AFCOOP. The filing is the annual report or financial statements plus a notarised member list, and late filing brings fines under Ley 356. Two corrections to the claim: Ley 845 Art. 4 was repealed by Ley 1140, and I found no fine amounts or recent enforcement news. No software or portal for this filing turned up. But the filing is a once-a-year handover of statements the co-op's accountant already prepares, plus a trip to the notary. A product adds little to that. The buyers are informal, union-like co-ops, so they are hard to reach and unlikely to pay. There are about 1,666 to 3,383 co-operatives, depending on the source.

The 2018 ASFI census was a one-off registration, and the 31 Jul 2018 deadline has passed. ASFI said it then handed oversight to the AEMP, which checks only Commercio Code formalities (the general commercial registry). I found no current recurring duty, such as a pledge-book, periodic report or licence renewal, and no 2025-26 rule specific to pawnshops. I found no competitor, but only 3 searches ran and none was a local vendor search. The universe is about 350 firms registered in 2018, which is small. The buyers are informal and the duty is weak, so the pain and the willingness to pay are both low.

Duty is real: AAPS licence/register regime under RAR 515/2017, with forms split at 10,000 inhabitants, plus PDQ plans and annual performance reporting. The 2023 indicators say AAPS regulated 88 EPSA and 74 met reporting requirements. The 2021 memoir says 43 EPSA were regularised. I did not open the primary sources, so I couldn't confirm penalties, deadlines or frequency. I found no commercial competitor. A 2018 GIZ-funded virtual platform for EPSA and AAPS existed, but its current status is unknown. The regulated base is small, at under 100 reporting EPSA. Committees are poor, and donors and NGOs (GIZ, Caritas) give free support. That makes willingness to pay and distribution weak. Score stays at 3.

The duty is real. DS 29165 (2007) requires producers, comercializadores and exportadores to hold a NIM, renewed annually, and to report their domestic sales and exports to Senarecom. The reporting mechanisms and deadlines are left to a regulation I did not find. Law 1503 and BCB RD 91/2026 (dated 29 Jun 2026, not 4 Dec 2025 as the claim says) let registered sellers sell gold to the BCB. I found no penalty, no company count and no competing software, but only 2 searches were run. Senarecom's own online system (SINACOM) takes the data upload, so the opportunity is thin. Buyers are a small, partly informal niche. The annual NIM renewal is a light workflow, and large firms handle the heavier export paperwork. Willingness to pay is unclear.

A 2009 SEDEGES regulation exists for creating and accrediting centres for ages 0-5. The national guidelines are still a proposal. A September 2026 UNICEF consultancy seeks help to adapt, update and "manage approval" of drafts from 2023 and 2025, so they are not approved and have no transition deadline. No software or state portal for this was found, but the duty is weak and enforcement is thin: SEDEGES has had no new staff for 14 years. There is no deadline-driven rush, and no register count was found. The buyers are scattered informal nurseries. Keep as a watch item and recheck when the guidelines are approved. Searches did not find the 2009 text itself or any count of centres.

result.duty: DGSC registration and local purchase authorisations for buying more than 120 L of diesel or imported gasoline off-tank (DS 5644 Arts. 15-16; earlier DS 28511 and DS 4910). Monthly tiers: 120-5,000 L from service stations; 5,000-19,999 L from storage plants. No penalties are specified for these articles.
result.market: Not quantified. A Correo del Sur article (2026-08-19) on large diesel consumers in Chuquisaca exists but was not opened. Over 80 private fuel importers were reported in 2025.
result.reason: DS 5644 Arts. 15-16 (and DS 4910/28511 before it) do require DGSC registration and local purchase authorisations above 120 L. But the DS 5644 text lists no sanctions for Arts. 4, 15 or 16. It takes effect only after an ANH resolution, and I could not confirm that resolution was issued. The Ministry of Government procedures are also unconfirmed. DS 5517 reportedly suspends diesel from controlled substances. The process is not clearly recurring, since renewal frequency is unknown. It is a state-run procedure with the DGSC as the gatekeeper. Buyers are scattered and not tech-ready. I found no competing software, but I searched for it only lightly. No market count was found. Overall: weak, uncertain duty, low software value.

Duty is likely real: AGEMED's 43-page Ministry of Health manual for psychotropics and narcotics (T-N-22-RM) is addressed to pharmacies, distributors and importers, under Ley 1737. I could not read the PDF text (the fetch returned binary), so I could not confirm the ledger format, reporting frequency, recipient, penalties or manual date. No Bolivian vendor or free state tool for this ledger turned up, but only two searches covered it. No pharmacy count found. AGEMED's online platform was reportedly down from 2 June 2026. Likely a small niche: paper books, thin willingness to pay, and a hard sale to individual pharmacies. Related known idea: K01.
